title: Pauline Permission, Benefit, Mastery, and Building Up
compression: All things are lawful, but not all things are constructive.
source_reconstruction: The working compression combines two related passages: 1 Corinthians 6:12 qualifies permission by benefit and by refusal to be mastered; 1 Corinthians 10:23 repeats the permission and benefit pattern and adds the criterion of building up.
assumption_envelope: The word lawful can over-suggest a modern juridical frame; permitted is another plausible rendering.
The attribution of the permission formula as a Corinthian slogan is an exegetical reconstruction rather than an explicit quotation marker in the Greek text.
The phrase not all things build up belongs to 1 Corinthians 10:23 rather than 6:12.
Constructive is a later English interpretive compression of the build-up image, not a direct lexical identity.
decoder_prerequisites: Distinguish source text from translation choice.
Distinguish translation from historical or speaker reconstruction.
Distinguish our later working compression from Paul's source wording.
Distinguish a later application from an attribution of original authorial intent.
candidate_invariants: Permission alone is not the only evaluative consideration in the two passages.
The later build-up criterion should remain distinct from the mastery criterion even when both inform a later compression.
cliffs: Do not say that 1 Corinthians 6:12 literally says not all things build up.
Do not store the Corinthian-slogan reading as uncontested fact.
Do not attribute later AI or organizational applications backward to Paul.

layers.notes: Machine-readable transliteration of the clauses highlighted in the worked specimen.

layers.content: All things are permitted or lawful for me; not all things are beneficial; I will not be mastered by anything.
Panta exestin; ou panta sympherei; ou panta oikodomei.
All things are permitted or lawful; not all things are beneficial; not all things build up.
Exestin is commonly rendered lawful or permitted; the English lawful can sound more narrowly juridical than the Greek requires.
Sympherei carries the sense of beneficial, profitable, advantageous, or helpful in context.
Oikodomei uses building language and is commonly rendered builds up or edifies.
A widespread scholarly reading treats the permission formula as a Corinthian slogan that Paul quotes and qualifies, while published scholarship also disputes the need for that attribution.
assumptions: Modern quotation marks can silently encode the slogan interpretation.

layers.content: Constructive became our compact working signal for what builds up rather than merely being permissible.
layers.notes: Useful compression, but not a literal rendering of 1 Corinthians 6:12.

layers.content: The distinction between mere permission and what builds up may inspire later thinking about AI or organizational design.
layers.notes: This is not attributed backward as Paul's own technical theory.

layers.content: The clause not all things build up belongs to 1 Corinthians 10:23, not to 1 Corinthians 6:12.
